chapters.title: Chapter 4: How Liquidity Moves Asset Classes

lessons.title: Equities and Liquidity: Why the Nifty and S&P Rally on QE and Wobble on QT

body.text: An equity rally has two engines: earnings growth and the multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. Liquidity works almost entirely through the second engine, the multiple, which is exactly why separating a liquidity-driven rally from an earnings-driven one is a core skill for reading markets.

body.caption: A stock or index's price return can be roughly decomposed into earnings growth and the change in the multiple the market pays for those earnings. Liquidity's main channel runs through the second term.

children.text: A standard equity valuation discounts future cash flows back to the present using a discount rate, built from a risk-free rate plus an equity risk premium. When the Fed runs QE, risk-free rates fall, and the search for yield in a liquidity-flush world tends to compress the risk premium too, since investors are more willing to take risk when safe assets pay so little. A lower discount rate mechanically raises the present value of the same future earnings, which is exactly what a higher P/E multiple represents. QT runs this in reverse: rates rise, risk appetite tightens, the discount rate rises, and the same future earnings are worth less today, showing up as multiple contraction.

body.text: Do not treat every P/E spike as multiple expansion driven by liquidity. In 2020, Nifty's trailing P/E spiked to unusually elevated levels, but a meaningful part of that spike was a denominator effect: reported earnings had collapsed due to the pandemic shock, mechanically inflating the P/E ratio even before liquidity-driven buying pushed prices up. Always check whether a P/E move is coming from the price (numerator) or from a temporary earnings collapse (denominator) before calling it a liquidity story.

body.title: Decompose the Return
body.prompt: The Nifty rose 25% over a year. Nifty EPS grew 8% over the same period. Using the approximation above, roughly what percentage of the Nifty's return came from multiple expansion rather than earnings growth?
body.explanation: Using %change in Price is approximately %change in Earnings plus %change in the multiple: 25% total return minus 8% earnings growth leaves roughly 17 percentage points attributable to multiple expansion. That is the liquidity-sensitive portion of the rally, the part most at risk of reversing if global liquidity tightens.

children.text: Why Growth Stocks Feel It More Than Value Stocks

Duration, a concept borrowed directly from bond investing, applies to equities too. A bond with cash flows far in the future is far more sensitive to a change in interest rates than a bond paying most of its cash flows soon. The same logic applies to stocks: a high-growth company whose earnings are expected mostly several years out has, in effect, a longer duration than a mature, cash-generating business paying most of its value back to shareholders today. That is why growth and long-duration sectors sell off harder in a QT phase, and re-rate harder in a QE phase, than defensive, cash-generative sectors.

columns.label: High-Duration (Growth, Small/Midcap, Unprofitable Tech)
points: Most of the expected earnings sit far in the future
Valuation is highly sensitive to the discount rate, so it re-rates sharply in both directions
Tends to lead a QE rally and lead a QT drawdown

columns.label: Low-Duration (FMCG, Utilities, PSU Banks, Dividend Payers)
points: Most of the value comes from near-term, steady cash flows
Valuation is comparatively insensitive to the discount rate
Tends to lag a QE rally but hold up better in a QT drawdown

children.text: Why FPI Flows Amplify the Liquidity Channel on the NSE and BSE

FPIs are typically the marginal, price-setting buyer or seller on the NSE and BSE at turning points, even though domestic mutual funds and retail investors on platforms like Zerodha hold a large and growing share of the market overall. When global liquidity expands, FPIs often lead the buying, particularly in the large, liquid names that make up the Nifty, which is why the Nifty's multiple tends to expand ahead of any pickup in domestic retail participation. This is a practical reason to track FPI flow data alongside Nifty valuations, rather than treating a rising Nifty and rising FPI inflows as two separate stories.

body.text: A useful habit, borrowed from fundamental analysis: before concluding a rally is justified, check the Nifty's or a stock's earnings trend on a tool like screener.in against its price move. If price is rising while trailing and forward earnings estimates are flat or falling, you are most likely looking at a liquidity-driven, multiple-expansion rally, not an earnings-driven one, and it carries more reversal risk if the global liquidity cycle turns.

body.title: Which Portfolio Holds Up Better?
body.scenario: Two fund managers are positioned very differently heading into a Fed-led QT cycle. Manager A is overweight high-growth, high-duration small and midcap names that led the previous QE-driven rally. Manager B is overweight FMCG, utilities and PSU banks with steady, near-term cash flows.
body.prompt: Based on the duration concept in this lesson, whose portfolio would you expect to hold up better as global liquidity tightens, and why might Manager A's positioning still make sense in a different part of the cycle?
body.modelAnswer: Manager B's low-duration, cash-generative portfolio would be expected to hold up better during a QT-driven tightening, because its valuation is far less sensitive to a rising discount rate, and most of its value comes from near-term cash flows rather than distant future earnings. Manager A's high-duration growth portfolio is more exposed to multiple contraction as rates and risk premiums rise, since a large share of its valuation rests on earnings expected years out. That said, Manager A's positioning is not wrong in general, it is simply suited to a different phase of the cycle: the same high-duration names that suffer most in QT are typically the ones that re-rate hardest and lead the rally once liquidity expansion resumes, which is why cycle-awareness, not a permanent stylistic bias, is the actual skill being tested here.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why do high-growth, long-duration stocks tend to fall more than defensive stocks during a quantitative tightening phase?
options: Because growth companies always have weaker earnings than defensive companies
Because their valuation depends heavily on earnings expected far in the future, making them more sensitive to a rising discount rate
Because the RBI specifically targets growth stocks during tightening
Because growth stocks are not listed on the NSE or BSE
body.explanation: A stock whose value depends mostly on earnings expected far in the future behaves like a long-duration bond: a rising discount rate reduces the present value of those distant cash flows more than it reduces the value of near-term cash flows, which is why growth and long-duration names see sharper multiple contraction in a QT phase.

points: Equity returns decompose roughly into earnings growth plus multiple expansion or contraction, and liquidity works almost entirely through the multiple.
QE lowers the discount rate (lower risk-free rates, compressed risk premium), raising valuations for the same earnings; QT reverses this.
Not every P/E spike reflects liquidity-driven multiple expansion; a collapse in earnings can mechanically inflate the P/E ratio too, as happened partly in 2020.
High-duration stocks (growth, small/midcap) are far more sensitive to the discount rate than low-duration stocks (FMCG, utilities, PSU banks), so they lead both QE rallies and QT drawdowns.

FPI flows tend to set the marginal price on the Nifty at turning points, which is why tracking FPI data alongside earnings trends (for example on screener.in) helps distinguish a liquidity-driven rally from an earnings-driven one.
